boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's capitulation of Trochtelfingen (18 October 1805) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group: the surrender of Werneck's corps to Murat's pursuit force by the capitulation signed at Trochtelfingen, from the summons sent after the action at Neresheim on 17 October to the signature and the dispute over the departed cavalry. The action at Neresheim the day before (B365b), the surrender of the battalions lost near Neresheim, the convoy fight near Zipplingen and the capitulations of detached troops at Kirchheim and Wallerstein the same day, and Archduke Ferdinand's escape to Öttingen are context, recorded where accounts count them together. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side B (Austrian) under FML Baron Werneck as 1,700 men, among them 4 generals and 71 officers, with 28 guns and 28 ammunition wagons, and prints no strength for side A (French) under Marshal Prince Murat. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. He prints no separate loss for this capitulation, and the passages read do not say which figures he used: by Krauss, Werneck stated that he had only 1500 infantry and about 100 riders left (claim werneck-figure), while Dupont's division journal gives the corps as 6,000 infantry and 800 cavalry (claim side-a-figures). English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: 'the French under Marshal Prince Murat force the Austrians (1,700 men [4 generals, 71 officers], 28 guns, 28 ammunition wagons) under FML Baron Werneck to surrender as prisoners of war'.

claims.value: Side B (Austrian) in Krauss: early on the 18th Werneck discovered that his cavalry had not camped at Trochtelfingen as ordered but had marched on by Marktoffingen toward Öttingen, so that by his own statement he had only 1500 infantry and about 100 riders left. Krauss says Archduke Ferdinand reached Öttingen that day with his cavalry, with Hohenzollern's and with some scattered infantry detachments of Werneck's corps.
claims.rationale: Werneck's own figure as Krauss reports it, read from the page image; Krauss's sentence on the Archduke was seen in the OCR. The figure is a commander's statement after the event, not a return. The corps reached Trochtelfingen as it stood after Neresheim, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'early on the 18th FML von Werneck discovered that his cavalry had not, as ordered, made camp at Trochtelfingen, but had marched on by Marktoffingen toward Öttingen. He thus had, by his statement, only 1500 men of infantry and about 100 riders at his disposal'; 'only Archduke Ferdinand reached Öttingen on 18 October with his cavalry, with that of FML Count Hohenzollern and with some scattered infantry detachments of Werneck's corps'.

claims.value: After the action at Neresheim (B365b) General Klein, having recognized the disintegration of the Austrian corps in the pursuit by Ohmenheim, sent a parlementaire to summon Werneck to lay down his arms, the corps being surrounded on all sides. Werneck's reply reached Klein as his column was about to march; Klein passed it to Murat, who sent his chief of staff, General Belliard, to settle the articles of the capitulation while he himself went on toward Nördlingen. The treaty Krauss prints is signed at Trochtelfingen by Belliard and Werneck. Klein then marched to the heights west of Öttingen to overawe the enemy and keep it from breaking the treaty. When Murat learned that the Austrian cavalry had gone, he would not recognize the treaty until the cavalry had submitted, and required Werneck to order Hohenzollern to submit.
claims.rationale: Decisions of side A's commanders as Krauss, the dragoon division's record and the cavalry reserve's report give them, all seen in the OCR; Krauss prints the signature from the Kriegsarchiv copy as 'Beillard'. English renderings (ours): Krauss, 'General Klein, who in the pursuit by Ohmenheim had recognized the disintegration of the Austrian corps, sent a parlementaire to FML Werneck with the summons to lay down his arms, as the Austrian corps was surrounded on all sides'; the record, 'General Klein received General Werneck's reply only at the moment when the column was about to set out; he at once had this letter passed to His Most Serene Highness Prince Murat, who sent General Belliard, chief of his staff, to settle the articles of the capitulation'; the report, 'His Highness, fearing for Nördlingen, pushed forward with his cavalry. On the way she received from Lieutenant General Werneck a reply to the summons that had been made to him. The general asked to capitulate. The Prince sent his chief of staff' (p. 1221) 'to Lieutenant General Werneck and continued his way toward Nördlingen' (p. 1222); Krauss, 'Trochtelfingen, 18 (OCR) October 1805. Beillard. Werneck, FML'; the record, 'General Klein then marched to the heights west of Öttingen, in order to overawe the enemy and prevent him from breaking his treaty'; Krauss, 'article 4 of the treaty was to bear bad fruit for FML von Werneck. When Murat learned of the departure of the Austrian cavalry, he would not recognize the whole treaty until the cavalry had submitted to the treaty. He therefore demanded of FML Werneck that he send an order to FML Count Hohenzollern to submit to the capitulation and so to surrender. FML von Werneck actually did this'.

claims.value: FML Werneck commanded side B. Met at Trochtelfingen by the parlementaire, he put off his decision to the next day, kept the French officer and gave the major of the Kaunitz regiment as a hostage. The dragoon division's journal says that in the night he moved his troops to the left of Nördlingen to join the Archduke at Öttingen, but that meeting French troops again they did not dare go on and came back to Trochtelfingen, whence he wrote to Klein that he was disposed to capitulate; Krauss gives Werneck's statement that he reconnoitred toward Kirchheim and Wallerstein in person in the night and met French troops there. Early on the 18th, his exhausted infantry being unable to escape the French cavalry without the support of strong cavalry, Werneck decided to capitulate. Article 4 of the capitulation bound the regiments and detachments separated from his corps as well; at Murat's demand he ordered Hohenzollern to submit. Krauss says Werneck later justified article 4 by his wish to obtain good terms and to ease the lot of the captive officers, and judges that he drew into the capitulation, for personal advantage, parts of his corps that could still have escaped.
claims.rationale: Side B's decisions as Krauss and the dragoon division's journal give them (OCR passages, except the decision to capitulate, read from the page image); Werneck's statements are his own account, and Krauss's judgment is an evaluation. English renderings (ours): Krauss, 'at Trochtelfingen they at last found Werneck, who reserved the decision for the 18th (OCR)'; the journal, 'but how great was his astonishment to meet, half a league (OCR) from this town, French patrols; he no longer doubted that the Austrians were surrounded, and the report he made of it to his general, whom he found at Trochtelfingen, determined him to listen to the proposal and to put off the conclusion to the next day; he kept the French officer and gave as hostage the major of the Kaunitz regiment'; 'nevertheless General Werneck had his troops make a movement during the night, to the left of Nördlingen, to join Archduke Ferdinand's corps at Öttingen; but having again met French troops, they did not dare to go further, and came back to take position at Trochtelfingen and the surroundings, whence General Werneck wrote to General Klein, sending back his parlementaire, to let him know that he was disposed to capitulate'; Krauss, 'FML von Werneck states that he reconnoitred in person in the night toward Kirchheim and Wallerstein and met French there'; 'as his exhausted infantry was not able, without the support of strong cavalry, to escape the French cavalry, Werneck decided early on the 18th to capitulate'; '4. All regiments, battalions, squadrons and detachments that are separated from the army corps of FML Werneck lay down their arms and become prisoners of war'; 'for he justified article 4 of the treaty in his reports by saying that he had wanted to obtain good terms of capitulation and to ease the fate of the captured officers!'; 'one does not know at which of the two generals one should wonder more, at Hohenzollern, who simply rides off by night with the cavalry and leaves in the lurch his corps commander, who was refusing the capitulation, and the infantry, to save himself, or at Werneck, who for the sake of personal advantages also includes in the capitulation parts of his corps that could still save themselves from it'; Murat's demand, as in claim side-a-command.

claims.value: Side B's account of its cavalry, in Krauss: it left in the night before the capitulation, against orders marching on toward Öttingen instead of camping at Trochtelfingen. Hohenzollern, ordered by Werneck to submit, replied that when he left Werneck, Werneck had in his presence refused any capitulation, that he had tried to save the cavalry and succeeded, and that since the day before he had been separated from Werneck and no longer took his orders. Krauss says Hohenzollern rode off by night with the cavalry and left his corps commander and the infantry in the lurch. Archduke Ferdinand, answering Hohenzollern from Schwabach, called the French general's claims illegal under the laws of war, declared that Hohenzollern and the troops who had come back with him could not be included in the capitulation, and ordered them to go on serving.
claims.rationale: Side B's account, from Krauss's page image, his OCR print of Hohenzollern's letter and the Archduke's letter as Alombert and Colin print it (OCR, t. III, vol. 2, p. 1256); both letters are the parties' own positions. It differs from the French reports on when and how the cavalry left (claim cavalry-departure-french); the passages read do not settle it. English renderings (ours): Krauss, as in claim werneck-figure; Hohenzollern, '"when I left you, you had in my presence refused any capitulation. I tried to save the cavalry; it succeeded"'; '"now, since yesterday, I am separated from you and it is no longer for me to follow your orders"'; Krauss's judgment as in claim side-b-command; the Archduke, 'you have submitted to me the letter of Lieutenant General Werneck; I shall answer you that according to the laws of war and the rights of nations I find the claims of the French general very illegal. Consequently I declare that you and the troops with which you came back cannot be included in the capitulation. I therefore order you, and them, to continue to serve as before'.

claims.value: Bodart records that the French forced side B to surrender as prisoners of war. By the first article of the capitulation Werneck's reserve corps laid down its arms, became prisoner of war and was to be taken to France; the officers were prisoners on parole and were to go to Austria, not to serve against the French or their allies until exchanged. The cavalry reserve's report gives the same terms. No source read gives a different result.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome with the capitulation's text as Krauss prints it from the Kriegsarchiv (article 1 read from the page image, article 2 and the signature in the OCR) and the cavalry reserve's report (page image). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Krauss, '1. The reserve corps under the command of FML Werneck lays down its arms, is prisoner of war and will be taken to France'; '2. The officers are prisoners of war on parole and go to Austria. Before an exchange has taken place they may fight neither against the French army nor against its allies'; the report, 'the arrangements were concluded, and according to the capitulation all the troops of the army corps of Lieutenant General Werneck are prisoners of war and sent back to France. The general and other officers may go home, on their word not to serve again until after being exchanged'.

claims.value: Werneck came to believe he was surrounded. The officer escorting the parlementaire met French patrols near Nördlingen and reported it; horsemen who had escaped from Weilermerkingen reported the capture of the battalion there by cavalry, which, the journal says, completed Werneck's persuasion; Krauss adds the result of Werneck's own reconnaissance toward Kirchheim, and says that this made him believe he was surrounded on all sides by strong French cavalry. Alombert and Colin say that the French Werneck met at nightfall near Kirchheim were General Milet's small dragoon depots from Nördlingen, supported by an infantry detachment with guns.
claims.rationale: Side B's information as Krauss, the dragoon division's journal and Alombert and Colin give it (OCR passages, except the footnote, read from the page image). open_questions: Deferred: the capitulation's original (Kriegsarchiv, 1805, Deutschland FA, X, 185 ad), which Krauss prints, and Werneck's reports and relation; the remainder of Dupont's division journal for 18 October after p. 1224 and Murat's own letters of the day; Krauss's map (Beilage 31). Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated in values: the hours of Murat's departure and of the gunfire; Alombert and Colin's figures for the convoy fight near Zipplingen and for Rivaud's prisoners (t. III, vol. 1, p. 100); the detachment of the 32e and its prisoners in Dupont's journal (p. 1224) and a dragoon brigade's capture on the way to the assembly point (p. 1221); the number of battalions that surrendered near Neresheim; the report's horse count on p. 1223.

Most consequential gap: what actually surrendered at Trochtelfingen. Bodart prints 1,700 men, 28 guns and 28 ammunition wagons; Werneck, by Krauss, had 1500 infantry and about 100 riders left; Dupont's journal gives 6,000 infantry and 800 cavalry; the cavalry reserve's 4,000 or 5,000 prisoners cover the whole day. A return of the prisoners handed over under the capitulation, or Krauss's appendix for the corps, could close it, and would also show whether Bodart's figure includes the detached troops bound by article 4.

Disputes kept as separate claims: when and how side B's cavalry left, and whether the capitulation bound it (Krauss and Hohenzollern's letter: before the capitulation, in the night before the 18th, and the Archduke's letter: not included in it; the French reports: after being told of it, against the faith of treaties); the strength figures above. The cavalry reserve's prisoner list names Hohenzollern and Mecsery, whom the same report says escaped.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked); Alombert and Colin, t. III (the French official history, printing the cavalry reserve's report, the dragoon division's record and journal and Dupont's division journal, all interested accounts, and the Archduke's letter to Hohenzollern; its introduction summarizes them); Krauss (an Austrian history printing the capitulation from the Kriegsarchiv and quoting Werneck's statements and Hohenzollern's letter, which are the parties' own accounts).
